diseaseName: Meningococcal Disease (Serogroups A, C, W, Y)
organism: Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus), an aerobic gram-negative bacterium closely related to N. gonorrhoeae. Its polysaccharide capsule is the key virulence factor, helping it resist phagocytosis and complement-mediated killing, and also defines its 12 known serogroups. Almost all invasive disease worldwide is caused by serogroups A, B, C, W, X, or Y; some strains lack a capsule entirely and are mainly associated with harmless nasopharyngeal carriage rather than invasive disease. This chapter covers the quadrivalent conjugate vaccines targeting serogroups A, C, W, and Y - see the companion Meningococcal B chapter for the separate serogroup B vaccines.
clinicalFeaturesSummary: Incubation period is typically 3-4 days (range 1-10). Meningitis is the most common presentation (about 50% of US cases): sudden fever, headache, and stiff neck, often with nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and altered mental status. Meningococcal septicemia without meningitis occurs in about 30% of cases, with abrupt fever, chills, cold extremities, severe pain, and a petechial or purpuric rash that can progress to shock, adrenal hemorrhage, and multiorgan failure. Bacteremic pneumonia accounts for another 15% and is the most common presentation in adults over 65. Case-fatality is 10%-15% even with appropriate antibiotics, and up to 20% of survivors have permanent sequelae such as hearing loss, neurologic damage, or limb loss.
epidemiologySummary: Humans are the only reservoir; about 10% of adolescents and adults are asymptomatic nasopharyngeal carriers at any time, mostly of nongroupable strains unlikely to cause disease. Transmission is via respiratory droplets or direct contact with respiratory secretions. Disease occurs year-round but peaks in late winter and early spring. Person-to-person communicability is generally limited - only 3%-4% of households with a case have a secondary case - though household contacts still face 500-800 times the general population's risk. US incidence in children and young adults under 24 is about 60% serogroup B (not covered by this vaccine group); college students specifically have more than 3 times the serogroup B risk of similarly aged non-students. Among people 24 and older, serogroups C, W, and Y together cause about 60% of cases.
secularTrendsSummary: US meningococcal disease incidence has declined steadily since a late-1990s peak; 329 total cases were reported in 2018 (0.10 per 100,000). Serogroups B and C are each responsible for roughly 25%-40% of US cases, with W and Y together with nongroupable strains making up another 5%-15% each - the proportion attributable to each serogroup varies substantially by age. About 95% of US cases are sporadic rather than outbreak-associated; 2010-2018 saw serogroup B outbreaks among university students and serogroup C outbreaks among men who have sex with men, among other affected communities.
vaccineDescription: Two quadrivalent (A, C, W, Y) meningococcal conjugate vaccines are currently licensed and available in the US: MenACWY-CRM (Menveo, ages 2 months-55 years, prepared in yeast-extract media) and MenACWY-TT (MenQuadfi, age 2+, the only one of the two approved for adults 56 and older). A third product, MenACWY-D (Menactra), was discontinued by its manufacturer in 2022, with remaining lots expiring by 2023, and is no longer available - Menveo now covers the under-2 age range Menactra used to serve. An older polysaccharide-only vaccine (Menomune) and a Hib-MenCY combination (MenHibrix) were discontinued earlier still. Both current vaccines are given intramuscularly and contain no adjuvant, antibiotic, or preservative (though formaldehyde is used during manufacturing). Two further pentavalent (A, B, C, W, Y) products also cover this serogroup group, bundled with a serogroup B vaccine - see 'Pentavalent (MenABCWY) Vaccines' below.
vaccinationScheduleSummary: Routine vaccination is recommended for all adolescents: first dose at 11-12 years, booster at 16. Those who get their first dose at 13-15 need a one-time booster, ideally at 16-18; those who get their first dose at 16 or older generally don't need a booster unless they later become high-risk. Routine vaccination of healthy people not otherwise at increased risk is not recommended after age 21. For people at increased risk (see Special Risk Groups), the schedule varies by specific risk factor and age, with boosters recommended every 3 years if the last dose was given before age 7, or every 5 years if given at 7 or older, for as long as increased risk continues. An older caveat about separating Menactra from PCV13 doses by at least 4 weeks in children with asplenia or HIV no longer applies in practice, since Menactra is discontinued and neither Menveo nor MenQuadfi carries that restriction.
vaccineEfficacySummary: Serum bactericidal antibody responses following MenACWY vaccination are generally high, but antibody levels wane over 3-5 years after a single dose - this waning, evidenced by declining seroprotection rates several years post-vaccination, is what drove ACIP's recommendation for a booster dose at age 16 following the primary adolescent dose at 11-12.
contraindicationsSummary: MenACWY vaccination is contraindicated for anyone who has had a severe allergic reaction after a previous dose of Menveo or MenQuadfi; after any component of those vaccines; or after any other meningococcal-, diphtheria toxoid-, tetanus toxoid-, or CRM197-containing vaccine (Menveo's ACWY components use a CRM197 carrier, a nontoxic diphtheria toxin derivative). Moderate or severe acute illness is a precaution. A history of Guillain-Barre syndrome was removed as an ACIP precaution for MenACWY vaccines in 2010 based on safety review. No randomized trials have evaluated MenACWY vaccination in pregnancy, but it is recommended for lactating women when otherwise indicated; when MenACWY is indicated during pregnancy or breastfeeding, either Menveo or MenQuadfi may be used.
vaccineSafetySummary: Local injection-site pain and erythema are common. Menveo: pain in 8%-54%, erythema in 12%-39%, with systemic reactions like irritability/drowsiness in infants and children and myalgia/headache/fatigue in adolescents and adults; a postlicensure study flagged a possible increased Bell's palsy risk within 84 days when Menveo was co-administered with other vaccines (not when given alone), but this was based on only 8 cases and its significance is uncertain. MenQuadfi: pain in 26%-45% after the primary dose, similar reactogenicity for boosters. Historical data on the now-discontinued Menactra (pain in 31%-69%, erythema in 3%-43%, no new safety signal across over 70 million distributed doses) is no longer clinically relevant since the product is off the market, but is retained here for anyone reconciling an older vaccination record.
vaccineStorageSummary: MenACWY vaccines must be stored at refrigerator temperature, 2C to 8C (36F to 46F); Menveo's lyophilized and liquid components should be stored together when possible. Menveo's lyophilized MenA component must be reconstituted only with Menveo's own liquid C-W-Y component - no other vaccine or diluent - and used immediately, or held at or below 25C (77F) for up to 8 hours if needed. See CDC's Vaccine Storage and Handling Toolkit for complete guidance.
surveillanceSummary: Meningococcal disease is reportable in all US states, and health care personnel should report any invasive case to local/state health departments immediately, since rapid chemoprophylaxis of close contacts depends on prompt identification of the index case. Diagnosis relies on culture (the gold standard) from a normally sterile site or PCR; once confirmed, serogrouping should follow via slide agglutination or real-time PCR - serologic antibody testing is not validated for clinical diagnosis or for deciding who needs vaccination. See CDC's Manual for the Surveillance of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases for reporting guidance.

supplementalTopics.title: Antimicrobial Chemoprophylaxis of Close Contacts
supplementalTopics.summary: The primary US strategy for preventing sporadic meningococcal disease is chemoprophylaxis of close contacts - household members, childcare contacts, and anyone directly exposed to the patient's oral secretions in the 7 days before symptom onset - given as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours of identifying the index case (prophylaxis given more than 14 days after onset is probably of little value). Rifampin, ciprofloxacin, and ceftriaxone are each 90%-95% effective at clearing nasopharyngeal carriage. Chemoprophylaxis is not indicated for contacts of noninvasive cases (isolated from a nonsterile site like the oropharynx) or for asymptomatic carriers. For air travel, prophylaxis is considered for anyone with direct exposure to an index patient's secretions, anyone seated next to them on a flight over 8 hours, or anyone within one seat in any direction if the index patient was coughing or vomiting.

supplementalTopics.title: Special Risk Groups Recommended for Vaccination
supplementalTopics.summary: Beyond routine adolescent vaccination, MenACWY is recommended starting as young as 2 months for anyone at increased risk: persistent complement component deficiencies (including eculizumab or ravulizumab-cwvz use), functional or anatomic asplenia (including sickle cell disease), HIV infection, microbiologists routinely exposed to N. meningitidis isolates, people identified by public health officials as at increased risk during an outbreak, and travelers to or residents of countries with hyperendemic or epidemic disease (notably the sub-Saharan African 'meningitis belt' or Saudi Arabia during Hajj/Umrah). The exact primary-series schedule and dosing interval depend on both the specific risk factor and the person's age at the time - infants starting Menveo at 8 weeks need a full 4-dose series, for example, while older children in most risk groups need only 1-2 doses.

supplementalTopics.title: Pentavalent (MenABCWY) Vaccines
supplementalTopics.summary: Two combination products now cover serogroups A, B, C, W, and Y in a single vaccine, for people who need both MenACWY and MenB at the same visit: MenACWY-TT/MenB-FHbp (Penbraya, Pfizer), licensed and ACIP-recommended since October 2023, and MenACWY-CRM/MenB-4C (Penmenvy, GSK), FDA-approved February 2025 and ACIP-recommended April 2025 - both licensed for ages 10-25. ACIP recommends either one, based on which serogroup B vaccine a person is already using, for two groups: healthy people 16-23 for whom shared clinical decision-making favors MenB vaccination (as a primary series), and people 10 or older at increased risk for meningococcal disease (as a primary series, or as a booster if their last MenABCWY or MenB dose was 6 or more months ago). The two pentavalent products are NOT interchangeable with each other, because their MenB components differ (MenB-FHbp vs. MenB-4C) - whichever brand of MenB-containing product a person has already received determines which pentavalent vaccine (if any) they should get next; see the companion Meningococcal B chapter's own Pentavalent entry for the MenB-side scheduling detail. Because Penmenvy's MenACWY-CRM component is conjugated to CRM197 (a diphtheria toxin derivative), it is additionally contraindicated for anyone with a severe allergic reaction history to a diphtheria toxoid-containing vaccine. Neither pentavalent product has high-quality pregnancy or breastfeeding safety data; if MenACWY is indicated during pregnancy or lactation, Menveo or MenQuadfi should be used instead of a pentavalent product.

keyPoints: As of 2021, five meningococcal vaccines were licensed in the US - three quadrivalent (A/C/W/Y) conjugate vaccines and two separate serogroup B vaccines; two pentavalent (A/B/C/W/Y) combination products have since been added, and one of the original three quadrivalent products (Menactra) has been discontinued
Menactra (MenACWY-D) was discontinued by its manufacturer in 2022; Menveo and MenQuadfi are the two quadrivalent products now available
About 10% of adolescents and adults carry N. meningitidis asymptomatically at any given time, mostly nongroupable strains that rarely cause disease
Case-fatality is 10%-15% even with treatment, and up to 20% of survivors have permanent sequelae
Antibody waning 3-5 years after a single adolescent dose is why a booster at age 16 was added to the routine schedule
Household contacts face 500-800 times the general population's risk, but overall person-to-person spread is still considered limited
Chemoprophylaxis of close contacts, not vaccination, is the primary tool for preventing sporadic (non-outbreak) disease
Two pentavalent MenABCWY vaccines now exist (Penbraya since 2023, Penmenvy since 2025) for people who need both MenACWY and MenB at once, but they are not interchangeable with each other
